courses.title: Anatomy
courses.description: Structure of the human body — upper limb, thorax and head & neck essentials.

courses.title: Physiology
courses.description: How organ systems work — cardiovascular, renal and respiratory physiology.

courses.title: Biochemistry
courses.description: Metabolism, enzymes and vitamins that underpin clinical medicine.

courses.title: Pharmacology
courses.description: Principles of drug action, autonomic drugs and antimicrobials.

topics.title: Brachial Plexus
topics.summary: Roots, trunks and the classic nerve injuries of the upper limb.

material.heading: Overview
material.body: The brachial plexus is formed by the anterior rami of C5–T1. It is organised as roots, trunks, divisions, cords and terminal branches, and supplies the skin and muscles of the upper limb.
keyPoints: Roots: C5, C6, C7, C8, T1
Cords are named by their relation to the axillary artery

material.heading: Terminal branches
material.body: Five terminal branches arise from the cords: musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves.
keyPoints: Axillary nerve — deltoid, teres minor; at risk in surgical neck fractures
Radial nerve — extensors; at risk in midshaft humerus fractures (wrist drop)
Ulnar nerve — most intrinsic hand muscles (claw hand)
Median nerve — thenar muscles (ape hand, carpal tunnel)

material.heading: Plexus injuries
material.body: Upper trunk injury (Erb's palsy, C5–C6) gives the "waiter's tip" posture. Lower trunk injury (Klumpke's palsy, C8–T1) affects the intrinsic hand muscles and may cause claw hand.

topics.title: Anatomy of the Heart
topics.summary: Chambers, valves, conducting system and coronary circulation.

material.heading: Chambers and surfaces
material.body: The heart has four chambers. The sternocostal (anterior) surface is formed mainly by the right ventricle, which makes it the most anterior chamber.

material.heading: Valves
material.body: Atrioventricular valves (tricuspid on the right, mitral on the left) separate atria from ventricles. Semilunar valves (pulmonary and aortic) guard the outflow tracts.

material.heading: Conducting system and blood supply
material.body: The sinoatrial node lies in the wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava. The left coronary artery divides into the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries. Most cardiac veins drain into the coronary sinus.

topics.title: Cranial Nerves
topics.summary: Functions and foramina of the twelve cranial nerves.

material.heading: Eye movements
material.body: Most extraocular muscles are supplied by the oculomotor nerve (CN III). The exceptions are superior oblique (trochlear, CN IV) and lateral rectus (abducens, CN VI).
keyPoints: Memory aid: LR6 SO4, the rest 3

material.heading: Face and tongue
material.body: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) supplies the muscles of mastication. Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue travels in the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII).

material.heading: Skull foramina
material.body: The glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X) and accessory (XI) nerves leave the skull through the jugular foramen. The hypoglossal nerve (XII) uses the hypoglossal canal.

topics.title: The Cardiac Cycle
topics.summary: Pressure and volume changes, heart sounds and cardiac output.

material.heading: Phases
material.body: Each cycle has systole (isovolumetric contraction, ejection) and diastole (isovolumetric relaxation, filling). During the isovolumetric phases all four valves are closed.

material.heading: Heart sounds
material.body: S1 is caused by closure of the atrioventricular (mitral and tricuspid) valves at the start of systole. S2 is caused by closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves.

material.heading: Cardiac output
material.body: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume. A typical resting stroke volume is about 70 mL, giving an output of about 5 L/min at 70 beats per minute.

topics.title: Renal Physiology
topics.summary: Filtration, tubular reabsorption and hormonal control.

material.heading: Glomerular filtration
material.body: Normal GFR is about 125 mL/min (about 180 L/day). The macula densa in the distal tubule senses NaCl delivery and helps regulate GFR through tubuloglomerular feedback.

material.heading: Tubular handling
material.body: The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs most filtered sodium, water, and almost all filtered glucose and amino acids.

material.heading: Hormonal control
material.body: ADH inserts aquaporin-2 channels in the collecting duct, increasing water reabsorption. Aldosterone increases sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion in the distal nephron.

topics.title: Respiratory Physiology
topics.summary: Lung volumes, control of breathing and oxygen transport.

material.heading: Lung volumes
material.body: Tidal volume at rest is about 500 mL. Residual volume is the air left after maximal expiration and cannot be measured by simple spirometry.

material.heading: Control of breathing
material.body: In healthy people the main chemical drive to breathe is arterial PCO₂, sensed mainly by central chemoreceptors through changes in CSF H⁺.

material.heading: Oxygen transport
material.body: Surfactant from type II pneumocytes reduces alveolar surface tension. The oxygen–haemoglobin curve shifts right with increased CO₂, H⁺, temperature and 2,3-BPG.

topics.title: Glycolysis
topics.summary: Steps, regulation and energy yield of glucose breakdown.

material.heading: Overview
material.body: Glycolysis converts glucose to pyruvate in the cytoplasm. Under anaerobic conditions pyruvate is reduced to lactate, regenerating NAD⁺.

material.heading: Regulation
material.body: Phosphofructokinase-1 (PFK-1) is the rate-limiting enzyme. Hexokinase and pyruvate kinase are the other irreversible steps.

material.heading: Energy and clinical links
material.body: Anaerobic glycolysis gives a net 2 ATP per glucose. Red cells depend on glycolysis, so pyruvate kinase deficiency causes haemolytic anaemia.

topics.title: Enzymes & Kinetics
topics.summary: How enzymes work and how inhibitors change their kinetics.

material.heading: How enzymes work
material.body: Enzymes speed up reactions by lowering the activation energy. They do not change the equilibrium of the reaction.

material.heading: Michaelis–Menten kinetics
material.body: Km is the substrate concentration at which the reaction rate is half of Vmax. A lower Km means higher affinity. Allosteric enzymes show sigmoidal rather than hyperbolic kinetics.

material.heading: Inhibition
material.body: Competitive inhibitors raise Km without changing Vmax. Non-competitive inhibitors lower Vmax without changing Km.

topics.title: Vitamins
topics.summary: Functions and deficiency states of key vitamins.

material.heading: Water-soluble vitamins
material.body: Thiamine (B1) deficiency causes beriberi and Wernicke encephalopathy. Niacin (B3) deficiency causes pellagra. Vitamin C deficiency causes scurvy.

material.heading: Fat-soluble vitamins
material.body: Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness. Vitamin K is required for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X.

material.heading: Bioavailability
material.body: Bioavailability is the fraction of a dose that reaches the systemic circulation unchanged. It is 100% for intravenous drugs. Oral drugs may undergo first-pass metabolism, mainly in the liver.

material.heading: Distribution and dosing
material.body: The loading dose depends on the volume of distribution. Steady state is reached after about 4–5 half-lives of regular dosing.

material.heading: Elimination kinetics
material.body: Most drugs follow first-order kinetics. A few, such as ethanol, follow zero-order kinetics — a constant amount is eliminated per unit time.

topics.title: Autonomic Drugs
topics.summary: Cholinergic and adrenergic agonists and antagonists.

material.heading: Cholinergic drugs
material.body: Atropine is a muscarinic antagonist. Organophosphates inhibit acetylcholinesterase; poisoning is treated with atropine and pralidoxime.

material.heading: Adrenergic drugs
material.body: Salbutamol is a β2 agonist used in asthma. Propranolol is a non-selective β blocker. Intramuscular adrenaline is the first-line treatment for anaphylaxis.

topics.title: Antimicrobials
topics.summary: Mechanisms and important adverse effects of antibiotics.

material.heading: Mechanisms
material.body: β-lactams such as penicillins inhibit bacterial cell wall synthesis. Aminoglycosides inhibit the 30S ribosomal subunit.

material.heading: Adverse effects to remember
material.body: Aminoglycosides are nephrotoxic and ototoxic. Chloramphenicol can cause grey baby syndrome. Rifampicin turns body fluids red-orange. Metronidazole with alcohol causes a disulfiram-like reaction.

questions.stem: The brachial plexus is formed by the anterior rami of which spinal nerves?
questions.explanation: The brachial plexus arises from the anterior rami of C5, C6, C7, C8 and T1. C1–C4 form the cervical plexus.

questions.stem: A newborn delivered with shoulder dystocia holds the arm adducted and internally rotated with the forearm pronated. Which posture is this?
questions.explanation: This is Erb's palsy from injury to the upper trunk (C5–C6), which produces the "waiter's tip" posture.

questions.stem: Which nerve is most at risk in a fracture of the midshaft of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve runs in the radial (spiral) groove of the humerus. Injury here causes wrist drop.

questions.stem: A fracture of the surgical neck of the humerus most commonly injures which nerve?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck with the posterior circumflex humeral artery. Injury weakens deltoid and teres minor.

questions.stem: Klumpke's palsy results from injury to which roots?
questions.explanation: Klumpke's palsy is a lower trunk injury (C8–T1), affecting the intrinsic muscles of the hand.

questions.stem: Where is the sinoatrial node located?
questions.explanation: The SA node lies in the wall of the right atrium near the opening of the superior vena cava.

questions.stem: The tricuspid valve lies between which two chambers?
questions.explanation: The tricuspid valve is the right atrioventricular valve. The mitral valve is on the left.

questions.stem: The left anterior descending artery is a branch of which vessel?
questions.explanation: The left coronary artery divides into the left anterior descending and circumflex arteries.

questions.stem: Which chamber forms most of the anterior (sternocostal) surface of the heart?
questions.explanation: The right ventricle forms most of the sternocostal surface, making it the most anterior chamber.

questions.stem: The great cardiac vein drains into the:
questions.explanation: The great cardiac vein runs with the LAD and drains into the coronary sinus, which opens into the right atrium.

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve supplies the lateral rectus muscle?
questions.explanation: Lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve (LR6). Palsy causes inability to abduct the eye.

questions.stem: The superior oblique muscle is supplied by the:
questions.explanation: Superior oblique is supplied by the trochlear nerve (SO4).

questions.stem: The muscles of mastication are supplied by the:
questions.explanation: The mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (V3) supplies the muscles of mastication.

questions.stem: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue is carried by the:
questions.explanation: Taste from the anterior two-thirds travels in the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve. General sensation is via the lingual nerve (V3).

questions.stem: Which cranial nerve passes through the jugular foramen?
questions.explanation: CN IX, X and XI pass through the jugular foramen. The hypoglossal nerve uses the hypoglossal canal.

questions.stem: The first heart sound (S1) is caused by:
options: Closure of the aortic and pulmonary valves
Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
questions.explanation: S1 marks the start of systole and is caused by closure of the atrioventricular valves.

questions.stem: During isovolumetric contraction:
options: Only the AV valves are open
Only the semilunar valves are open
questions.explanation: Pressure rises in a closed ventricle — both AV and semilunar valves are closed, so volume does not change.

questions.stem: A typical resting stroke volume in an adult is about:
questions.explanation: Resting stroke volume is about 70 mL. At 70 beats/min this gives a cardiac output of about 5 L/min.

questions.stem: Cardiac output is calculated as:
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume.

questions.stem: The "a" wave of the jugular venous pulse corresponds to:
questions.explanation: The a wave is produced by right atrial contraction. It is absent in atrial fibrillation.

questions.stem: Most filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the:
questions.explanation: Almost all filtered glucose is reabsorbed in the proximal convoluted tubule via SGLT transporters.

questions.stem: A normal adult glomerular filtration rate is approximately:
questions.explanation: Normal GFR is about 125 mL/min, or roughly 180 L/day.

questions.stem: ADH increases water reabsorption mainly by acting on the:
questions.explanation: ADH acts on V2 receptors in the collecting duct to insert aquaporin-2 channels.

questions.stem: Aldosterone acts on the distal nephron to:
options: Increase sodium reabsorption and potassium secretion
questions.explanation: Aldosterone increases ENaC and Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity, so sodium is reabsorbed and potassium secreted.

questions.stem: The macula densa senses:
options: Blood pressure in the afferent arteriole
NaCl concentration in the distal tubule
questions.explanation: The macula densa senses tubular NaCl and drives tubuloglomerular feedback and renin release.

questions.stem: Normal resting tidal volume in an adult is about:
questions.explanation: Resting tidal volume is about 500 mL (roughly 7 mL/kg).

questions.stem: In a healthy person the main chemical stimulus for breathing is:
questions.explanation: Arterial PCO₂, acting through CSF H⁺ on central chemoreceptors, is the main drive. Hypoxic drive matters more when PO₂ is very low.

questions.stem: Surfactant is produced by:
questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes secrete surfactant, which reduces surface tension and prevents alveolar collapse.

questions.stem: Which shifts the oxygen–haemoglobin dissociation curve to the right?
questions.explanation: Increased 2,3-BPG, CO₂, H⁺ and temperature shift the curve right, helping oxygen unloading in tissues.

questions.stem: Which lung volume cannot be measured by simple spirometry?
questions.explanation: Residual volume stays in the lungs and needs helium dilution or body plethysmography to measure.

questions.stem: The rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis is:
questions.explanation: PFK-1 is the main control point, activated by AMP and fructose-2,6-bisphosphate and inhibited by ATP and citrate.

questions.stem: The net ATP yield of anaerobic glycolysis per glucose molecule is:
questions.explanation: 4 ATP are produced but 2 are used in the preparatory phase, giving a net 2 ATP.

questions.stem: Glycolysis takes place in the:
questions.explanation: All glycolytic enzymes are cytoplasmic.

questions.stem: Under anaerobic conditions in skeletal muscle, pyruvate is converted to:
questions.explanation: Lactate dehydrogenase reduces pyruvate to lactate, regenerating NAD⁺ so glycolysis can continue.

questions.stem: Which enzyme deficiency of glycolysis classically causes haemolytic anaemia?
questions.explanation: Red cells rely on glycolysis for ATP. Pyruvate kinase deficiency reduces ATP and causes haemolysis.

questions.stem: A competitive inhibitor:
options: Has no effect on Km or Vmax
questions.explanation: A competitive inhibitor competes for the active site. More substrate overcomes it, so Vmax is unchanged but Km rises.

questions.stem: Km is defined as the substrate concentration at which:
options: The rate is half of Vmax
questions.explanation: Km is the substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity. A low Km means high affinity.

questions.stem: A non-competitive inhibitor:
options: Binds only at the active site
questions.explanation: Non-competitive inhibitors bind away from the active site, reducing Vmax without changing Km.

questions.stem: Enzymes increase the rate of reactions by:
questions.explanation: Enzymes lower the activation energy. They do not change the equilibrium of the reaction.

questions.stem: Allosteric enzymes typically show which velocity–substrate curve?
questions.explanation: Cooperative binding in allosteric enzymes gives a sigmoidal curve.

questions.stem: Scurvy is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin C is needed for collagen hydroxylation. Deficiency causes bleeding gums and poor wound healing.

questions.stem: Wernicke encephalopathy is caused by deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Thiamine deficiency, often with chronic alcohol use, causes Wernicke encephalopathy: confusion, ophthalmoplegia and ataxia.

questions.stem: Pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia) is due to deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Pellagra is caused by niacin (B3) deficiency.

questions.stem: Vitamin K is required for:
options: γ-carboxylation of factors II, VII, IX and X
questions.explanation: Vitamin K is a cofactor for γ-carboxylation of clotting factors II, VII, IX and X (and proteins C and S).

questions.stem: Night blindness is an early sign of deficiency of:
questions.explanation: Vitamin A is needed to form rhodopsin in rod cells.

questions.stem: With regular dosing, steady-state concentration is reached after about:
questions.explanation: About 94–97% of steady state is reached after 4–5 half-lives.

questions.stem: First-pass metabolism of oral drugs occurs mainly in the:
questions.explanation: Drugs absorbed from the gut go through the portal vein to the liver before reaching the systemic circulation.

questions.stem: Which of the following follows zero-order elimination kinetics?
questions.explanation: Ethanol is eliminated at a constant rate because alcohol dehydrogenase is saturated at usual concentrations.

questions.stem: The bioavailability of a drug given intravenously is:
questions.explanation: An IV dose goes straight into the systemic circulation, so bioavailability is 100% by definition.

questions.stem: The loading dose of a drug mainly depends on its:
questions.explanation: Loading dose = Vd × target concentration ÷ bioavailability. The maintenance dose depends on clearance.

questions.stem: Atropine acts as a:
questions.explanation: Atropine competitively blocks muscarinic receptors, e.g. treating bradycardia and organophosphate poisoning.

questions.stem: The first-line drug for anaphylaxis is:
questions.explanation: IM adrenaline is first-line. Antihistamines and steroids are adjuncts.

questions.stem: Propranolol is best described as a:
questions.explanation: Propranolol blocks both β1 and β2 receptors, so it is used with caution in asthma.

questions.stem: Along with atropine, which drug is used in organophosphate poisoning to reactivate acetylcholinesterase?
questions.explanation: Pralidoxime regenerates acetylcholinesterase if given before the enzyme "ages".

questions.stem: Salbutamol relieves bronchospasm by acting as a:
questions.explanation: Salbutamol stimulates β2 receptors on bronchial smooth muscle, causing bronchodilation.

questions.stem: Penicillins act by inhibiting:
questions.explanation: β-lactams bind penicillin-binding proteins and block peptidoglycan cross-linking in the cell wall.

questions.stem: The major adverse effects of aminoglycosides are:
questions.explanation: Aminoglycosides such as gentamicin are nephrotoxic and ototoxic, so levels are monitored.

questions.stem: Grey baby syndrome is associated with:
questions.explanation: Newborns cannot conjugate chloramphenicol well, so it accumulates and causes circulatory collapse.

questions.stem: Which drug turns urine and tears red-orange?
questions.explanation: Rifampicin colours body fluids red-orange. Patients should be warned.

questions.stem: Taking alcohol with which antibiotic can cause a disulfiram-like reaction?
questions.explanation: Metronidazole inhibits aldehyde dehydrogenase, causing flushing, nausea and vomiting with alcohol.

news.title: Post-UTME season: what aspiring medical students should prepare
news.summary: Screening windows open at different times for each school. Here is a checklist so you are ready when yours does.
body: Each university sets its own post-UTME or screening timetable, and medicine is usually one of the most competitive courses. Check your chosen school’s official admissions portal regularly rather than relying on forwarded messages.
Have these ready: your UTME result slip, O’level results (with the right subject combination for medicine), passport photographs, and a working email address and phone number.
Only pay fees through the official portal, and keep every receipt and printout until admission is confirmed.

news.title: Scholarship season: how to find awards open to medical students
news.summary: Government, state, corporate and alumni scholarships all accept medical students. Deadlines are tight, so start early.
body: Many scholarships for Nigerian undergraduates open once a year, and several give extra weight to students in medicine and other health sciences.
Look at four places: your state scholarship board, corporate foundations, your faculty’s alumni association, and notices from your school’s student affairs office.
Keep a scanned copy of your admission letter, latest results and a reference letter so you can apply within a day of a call going out.

news.title: Starting clinical postings? A first-week checklist
news.summary: Moving from the lecture hall to the wards is a big step. These habits help you settle in quickly.
body: Arrive early for your first ward round, introduce yourself to the resident doctors, and find out how clerking is shared among your group.
Carry a small notebook for cases you see. Reviewing them against your textbook the same evening is one of the fastest ways to learn.
Keep practising topic questions on EdMira alongside your postings so the theory keeps pace with what you see on the ward.

news.title: Professional exams: building a revision plan that works
news.summary: Spread revision across every course, practise past-question styles, and track your weak topics week by week.
body: Start by listing every course in your coming professional exam and how confident you feel in each one.
Spend more time on your weakest topics, but touch every course each week so nothing goes cold.
Use the Progress tab to see which topics are averaging under 60% and revisit them first.

news.title: Semester resumption: where to find your school’s official calendar
news.summary: Resumption and exam dates change often. Here is how to avoid acting on outdated or fake notices.
body: Rely on your university’s official website, registrar’s notices and your faculty’s verified class channels for resumption and exam dates.
Be wary of screenshots with no date or source. If in doubt, confirm with your class representative or faculty office.
